solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Car bullies nip to when out for spin

indicators.note: out here means out of order or wrong, so the letters of car bullies nip to are rearranged

explanation.surface: Aggressive drivers dart out for a quick drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges CAR BULLIES NIP TO. 'spin' looks like a car outing, but it is the slanted presentation of news.
explanation.definitionFit: Spin is the favourable slant put on information by press officers and image managers.

clue.text: Quiet individual in red, say

parts.note: p (piano) is quiet in music
someone in the red owes money: an ower

explanation.surface: Someone murmurs about a quiet person dressed in red.
explanation.walkthrough: "Say" looks like the usual 'for example' tag, but it is the noun: to have a say is to have power over a decision.
explanation.definitionFit: Say is used in its noun sense of influence over a decision, a near synonym.

clue.text: Everyone has issue with British writer

parts.note: standard abbreviation
everyone = all
an issue under discussion is a point

explanation.surface: A British author is at odds with the whole world.
explanation.walkthrough: The "writer" is not an author but a pen.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballpoint is a pen, something you write with.

clue.text: Knight one recalled as a bit of a looker

indicators.note: called back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a knight's title
roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A knight is remembered as rather handsome.
explanation.walkthrough: "A looker" suggests an attractive person; here it is an eye, and the iris is a part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The iris is part of the eye, the organ that looks.

clue.text: Cattle poisoner in paper with men to get time

parts.note: a rag is a downmarket newspaper
w is short for with
other ranks: soldiers who are not officers
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about a cattle poisoner who gets a prison term.
explanation.walkthrough: Ragwort is a yellow-flowered weed that is toxic to livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragwort poisons cattle and horses that eat it.

clue.text: Regrets fast times being over in the morning

indicators.note: the fasts sit over, so around, the morning

parts.note: Lent is a fast; several of them are Lents
am = ante meridiem, the morning

explanation.surface: Someone rues staying up late until the early hours.
explanation.walkthrough: "Fast times" reads as wild living; it means periods of fasting.
explanation.definitionFit: To lament something is to regret it.

clue.text: Extremely thuggish cur seizing larynx primarily?

definitions.text: Extremely thuggish cur seizing larynx primarily?

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters, so only the ends of thuggish are kept

parts.note: the word whose outer letters are kept

indicators.note: seizing means grabbing hold, so the cur holds the next letter inside it

parts.note: a rotter is a cur, a contemptible person

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of larynx is used

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A brutish lout grabs someone by the voice box.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: someone who seizes a person's larynx is a strangler. 'Extremely' gives TH and 'primarily' gives the L that 'seizing' tucks into ROTTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A throttler strangles a victim by the throat, exactly the act of a thug grabbing the windpipe.

clue.text: Yellowy-orange line one mustn't cross banking river

indicators.note: the line holds the river as a bank holds its money

parts.note: the oche is the line a darts player must stand behind
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A painted line by a river that nobody may step over.
explanation.walkthrough: The oche is the throwing line in darts, a pub game popular in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is an earthy yellow-orange pigment and colour.

clue.text: Developing harms last low-lying wetland

indicators.note: developing means changing form as it grows, so the letters of harms last are rearranged

explanation.surface: Building work damages the last remaining marshy ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Developing' rearranges HARMS LAST, and in the surface property development is what harms the wetland.
explanation.definitionFit: A salt marsh is coastal ground regularly flooded by the tide, a flat boggy habitat.

clue.text: Welsh wicked at home, having good game

parts.note: standard abbreviation
ill as in evil, ill will
at home = in
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A Welsh team plays badly at home but has a good match.
explanation.walkthrough: "Game" looks like a match; it is the adjective, as in 'game for anything'.
explanation.definitionFit: Game is the informal adjective for eager to take part, a plain synonym.

clue.text: First of howitzers coming in alarms new officer

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so the combined letters are put in a new order
coming in means entering, so the letter goes into the word alarms before the mix

parts.note: taken as written, the bulk of the letters to be mixed

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: Artillery fire arriving sets off alarms for a newly commissioned officer.
explanation.walkthrough: The H from 'First of howitzers', 'coming in' to ALARMS, makes a pool of seven letters that 'new' rearranges. 'Howitzers' and 'officer' paint an army scene, which suits the answer's field-marshal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A marshal is a high-ranking officer, as in field marshal, or a law-enforcement official in the US.

clue.text: Spending grand on beef can be excessive

indicators.note: money spent is gone, so the grand is removed

parts.note: a beef is a complaint, a gripe
a grand is a thousand pounds, G

explanation.surface: Paying a thousand for a cut of beef is too much.
explanation.walkthrough: "Beef" is a grumble, not meat, and a grand (£1,000) is G; language called a bit ripe is over the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripe can mean coarse or overdone, as in a ripe remark, which is excessive.

clue.text: A worm tends to go with the flow

indicators.note: to go means to go astray, so the letters of a worm tends are rearranged

explanation.surface: A worm likes to drift along with the current.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go' rearranges A WORM TENDS; 'tends to go' reads as one phrase in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Downstream means in the direction a river's current runs.

clue.text: Reportedly do this to slow nag or dog

indicators.note: as reported, so as it is spoken

parts.note: a jockey whips a slow horse

explanation.surface: Advice on what to do with a lazy horse, or a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: A nag is a worn-out horse; say "whip it" and you hear the racing dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The whippet is a slim, fast dog bred for racing.

clue.text: Deliberately annoying ending

definitions.meaning: to wind someone up is to tease them on purpose
closing down a meeting or a company

explanation.surface: A finale meant to irritate.
explanation.walkthrough: Wind someone up is British for teasing or provoking them deliberately.
explanation.definitionFit: Winding up is both teasing someone on purpose and bringing something to a close.

clue.text: Meander around with other posers at front?

definitions.text: Meander around with other posers at front?

indicators.note: around here means turned about and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, most of the letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: the front of each word is its first letter

parts.note: the two words whose first letters are taken

explanation.surface: People wander about while show-offs strut along at the head of the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: to stroll about on a seafront among others who are showing off is to take a leisurely walk. The first letters of 'other posers' join MEANDER before the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A promenade is a leisurely stroll, often along a seafront where people go to see and be seen.

clue.text: Bright yellow ruined plush fur female binned

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the letters of plush fur are rearranged
binned means thrown away, so the female letter is discarded from the mix

explanation.surface: A luxurious yellow fur coat is spoiled and a woman throws it out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'binned' discards F from PLUSH FUR, and 'ruined' rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Sulphur is a pale vivid yellow, named after the colour of the element.

clue.text: Thumb your way through Amsterdam?

definitions.meaning: not leafing through a guidebook but holding out a thumb for lifts
just an example destination, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: Finding your way around Amsterdam with your nose in a guidebook.
explanation.walkthrough: "Thumb your way through" suggests leafing through a book, like a city guide; hitchhikers thumb their way instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To hitchhike is to travel by thumbing lifts from passing drivers.

clue.text: Thoughts and proposals lead to change for knight

indicators.note: the leading letter is swapped for another

parts.note: motions are proposals put to a meeting
N is the knight in chess notation, replacing M

explanation.surface: Ideas and suggestions that end in someone being knighted.
explanation.walkthrough: The lead letter M of MOTIONS gives way to N.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: ideas held in the mind.

clue.text: Going down is what I do when working

definitions.meaning: what the sun does in the evening
I is the crossword compiler, whose work is compiling puzzles

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they sink when they get to work.
explanation.walkthrough: "I" is the crossword setter speaking: a setter's work is setting puzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: The sun is setting as it goes down, and a setter at work is setting.

clue.text: Small problem keeping Republican in nick

parts.note: standard abbreviation

indicators.note: the problem holds the letter inside

parts.note: a hidden problem is a catch
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A minor issue: a Republican locked up in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: "Nick" looks like British slang for prison; here it is a small cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick in its sense of a small cut or mark on a surface is a plain synonym.

clue.text: In which one on the blue might want to sink?

definitions.meaning: not a sailor at sea but a player whose next ball is the blue
not to go under but to pot the ball into a pocket

explanation.surface: Someone out on the open sea wishes to go under.
explanation.walkthrough: "On the blue" suggests at sea and "sink" drowning; in snooker, a player lining up the blue ball wants to sink it in a pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: Snooker is the cue game where coloured balls, including the blue, are sunk.

clue.text: Piano featuring in popular piece for tour?

parts.note: in = fashionable

indicators.note: the piano appears inside the piece

parts.note: a piece of something is a section
p is piano, soft in music

explanation.surface: A piano solo in a crowd-pleasing work on a concert tour.
explanation.walkthrough: The P sits inside SECTION, after its S.
explanation.definitionFit: A tour of inspection is a visit to look things over, as in a tour of the premises.

clue.text: Standpoints of parties

definitions.meaning: opposing groups in a dispute or match

explanation.surface: The positions taken by rival political parties.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves mean the same word in slightly different senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A side is both a point of view and a group opposing another.

clue.text: Second part of this appears in broadcast?

definitions.text: Second part of this appears in broadcast?

indicators.note: a letter that appears in a word is placed inside it

parts.note: to broadcast seed is to sow it, scattering it widely

indicators.note: the second part of a word here is its second letter

parts.note: the word whose second letter is taken

explanation.surface: A question about which segment of a programme goes out on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' does two jobs: as a verb about scattering seed it gives SOW, and as a noun it defines the whole answer, a programme put out on air.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcast is a television or radio programme, which is a show.

clue.text: Comic performing in part of train

parts.note: a wag is a joker
on stage, performing

explanation.surface: A comedian doing a set aboard a train.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a wagon is a railway goods truck.
explanation.definitionFit: A wagon is a single truck forming part of a freight train.

clue.text: God is quietly unobtrusive, I hear

indicators.note: what I hear is the sound, not the spelling

parts.note: low-key means quiet and unobtrusive

explanation.surface: A remark that a deity keeps a low profile.
explanation.walkthrough: Loki, the Norse trickster god, is anything but low-key, which is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Norse trickster deity.

clue.text: Old leader plus a fellow that soldier locks up

indicators.note: the soldier holds the other letters inside

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
to add is to plus
used as it stands
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A former ruler and a companion are jailed by a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: Muammar Gaddafi ruled Libya until 2011.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaddafi was the long-time leader of Libya, now dead.

clue.text: Wise man wrapping present

indicators.note: the man is wrapped around the present

parts.note: the king is a man in chess
the present moment, now

explanation.surface: One of the three wise men bringing a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: "Wise man" and "present" suggest the Magi with gifts; the definition is just "Wise", and "present" is time, not a gift.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: shrewd, showing understanding.

clue.text: Old winger seeing gap's prone to move

indicators.note: to move means to shift around, so the letters of seeing gap's prone are rearranged

explanation.surface: A veteran footballer on the wing spots an opening and tends to run into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to move' rearranges SEEING GAPS PRONE. 'winger' looks like a footballer, but it is a bird, and 'Old' because it is extinct.
explanation.definitionFit: The passenger pigeon was a North American bird, once abundant, extinct since 1914.
